meta.title: Sundog Agility: Skill Library
meta.notes: Only material from Sundog Agility: Foundation class notes (Weeks 2–18, 2021–22), Puppy Kindergarten notes (Weeks 1–4, 2022), the Week 13 lap-turn diagram, the Week 13/14 videos, and the Week 5 toy-drive handout (Susan Garrett article distributed in class). Personal notes and outside links are kept separately. 'level': 1 start here, 2 building, 3 advanced.

skills.name: Training session basics
skills.purpose: How every session should be set up so the dog learns quickly and enjoys it.
how_to: Keep sessions short; spread games across the day or week instead of doing everything at once (e.g. 1 minute of Name Game before a meal).
Each exercise uses about 5–8 treats/rewards, then that session is done.
Prepare first: treats cut to size, toys, target plates, etc. all ready before you start.
Young or easily distracted dogs: train somewhere quiet, away from other pets and kids. Older dogs with skills: add mild distractions (yard, park).
Foundation class: do all exercises on leash so the dog stays connected to you.
Train when you're in a good mood. Be positive and fun; you're a team.
Start each session with warm-ups (see Warm-ups).
tips: Immediate rewards = faster learning, fewer repetitions, longer retention, faster performance. Late rewards = slow or no learning.
You have about 1 second for a reward or consequence to make sense to the dog (PK3).

skills.name: Positive reinforcement & finding what your dog values
skills.purpose: Training is play: find what your dog values most and use games to show they get it by playing with you and making the right choices.
how_to: List what your dog will work for: food, toys, praise, play.
Reward immediately when the dog makes the right choice.
Avoid confrontation and verbal corrections. Control access to rewards instead (e.g. closing your hand, closing the crate door).
tips: Dogs always do what's rewarding. The goal is teaching that rewards come through doing things with/for you, not by helping themselves (PK3).
Motivators: food drive, toy drive, prey drive. Each has pros and cons. Aim for a balance so the dog is both handler-focused and obstacle-focused, and can work at a distance (F03).

skills.name: Using verbal cues
skills.purpose: Rules for choosing and using cue words so they mean something the first time.
how_to: Pick short words that make sense to you and use them consistently.
Say a cue once (maybe twice if the dog is really struggling), then help with a lure rather than repeating it.
Build value for each word with great rewards (food/toys).
Choose one release word and stick with it. Short words are easier to say while running.
tips: Dogs respond to body language first, words second. Body language usually overrides verbals. 'Less is more': save verbals for things that matter.
See the Cue Glossary for every word used in the classes.

skills.name: Warm-ups
skills.purpose: Get the dog focused, engaged and in the right arousal level before work.
how_to: Start every session with something fun: stretches, known tricks, basic obedience, tug, Push Away and Run.
If the dog is too high to think: use calm but fun warm-ups or calming games.
If the dog is flat: rev them up with exciting play, then ask for focused work.

skills.name: Teaching 'Yes' (marker word)
skills.purpose: 'Yes' means the exercise is over and a reward is coming right now.
how_to: Say 'Yes', feed a treat. Repeat until the treats are gone.
tips: 'Good' is different: it means keep going, you're doing it right (continue the exercise).
Words can carry emotion (excited or disappointed tone); a clicker always sounds the same (F06).

skills.name: Charging the clicker
skills.purpose: Teach the dog that the click always means a treat is coming.
how_to: Have a handful of really good treats cut small.
Click once, then feed. The treat follows the click, not at the same time. Click > treat, click > treat.
Don't point the clicker at the dog like a remote; hold it at your side or behind your back.
Repeat standing, sitting, moving, and in different places.
A few times a day, 6–10 treats each. Done when the dog visibly anticipates the treat at the click.

skills.name: Shaping & capturing
skills.purpose: Build behaviours from scratch, with no physical control or corrections, by marking small steps toward a goal.
equipment: novel objects: pizza box, book, mat, pot, box, perch
how_to: Capturing: wait for the dog to do the whole behaviour (e.g. sit), mark and reward it, then add a cue once it happens often.
Shaping: mark and reward successive small steps toward the final behaviour.
Novel-object starter (F07): put an object down, stare at it. No words, no luring. Click & feed for looking at it, moving toward it, nose-touching it, a foot on it.
Raise criteria gradually. At each new level reward every time for a handful of reps, then reward randomly, then raise criteria again.
Add the cue only once the final behaviour is reliable; then reward only cued reps.

progressions.text: Free interaction with novel objects (look, approach, nose, foot).
Specific behaviours: one foot on the board, four feet on the board, nose touch.
Clicker challenge: all 4 feet in a box, OR front feet on 2 separate objects (e.g. 2 small books). Also review nose touch on an object.
Rotate challenges between sessions (nose touch one session, box work the next). Bring items to class to demo.

examples.name: Ring a bell (to ask to go out)
steps: Hang the bell where you want it (e.g. by the door).
Start near the bell; wait and watch.
Click & feed for looking at the bell; reward a few looks.
Raise criteria: one step toward the bell.
Keep raising: closer and closer, then only touching it.
Then only reward loud rings, not feeble ones.
Add the cue; if it's for potty, use going outside as the reward.

tips: Shaping needs good observation and timing; it's the more advanced method.
The more you shape, the more the dog offers behaviours, and the faster new things are learned.
Shaping builds a thinking dog that keeps working through hard problems, plus mental stamina and body awareness.

Trick ideas from the notes: back up, left/right spins, hand touch, weave between legs, sit up, paw touch, chin rest, take a nap, go to bed, play dead, roll over, lights on/off, open a drawer/door, put away toys, fetch keys/remote/blanket.
Video: shaping a 12-week puppy to back onto an object: https://youtu.be/CpA25qUBxiA

skills.name: The Shaping Game (practice with people)
skills.purpose: Practise clicker timing on a human 'dog' and feel how hard it is to learn without words.
how_to: 2+ people. One is the 'dog' and leaves the room; the rest pick a behaviour (turn on a light, sit on the floor with hands on head…).
One trainer, one 'dog'. No words, gestures, sounds or eye hints.
Click for movement in the right direction/closer to the goal, like 'hot and cold'.
tips: Shows how a late click leads to the wrong behaviour.

skills.name: Cookie fingers
skills.purpose: A signal that means 'come to this hand, there's food'. The basis for luring and for many handling moves.
how_to: Treat in hand, held at the dog's nose height.
Shake your wrist up and down as you move; the dog follows your hand.
Practise on both sides.
tips: Teaches your dog to pay attention to your body language and the value of your hand. It's the beginning step for many agility handling moves.
For handling, keep cookie fingers low, by your knee (Week 13).

skills.name: Hand targeting ('Touch')
skills.purpose: Nose-to-palm touch. A portable focus tool, a distraction from trouble, and the first step toward contact training.
how_to: Put a handful of small treats in one hand. In the other, hold one treat between two fingers of an open palm.
Present the open palm so the dog sees/smells the treat.
When the nose touches the palm, say 'Yes' as the dog eats the treat.
Wean the finger treat; present an empty palm and add 'Touch'. When the dog bumps it, reward by presenting the treat on the palm where they touched.

progressions.text: Treat between fingers > empty palm with 'Touch'.
Goal: firm 'bird-peck' touches at different heights and angles: low, away from your body, up on hind legs.
Use a small plastic target held in the hand; add 'Touch'/'Target' once the dog touches reliably when it's offered.

tips: A great way to distract or refocus your puppy.

skills.name: Push Away and Run
skills.purpose: Dogs want what they can't have; make that you.
how_to: Gently push the dog away on the chest or side.
Run away and call.
When the dog catches up, reward with food, a toy, or lots of play.

skills.name: 'Find' / 'Scatter' (treats on the ground)
skills.purpose: Permission to scavenge for a moment. Gets attention, removes attention from something else, and resets the dog's position.
how_to: 'Find'/'Search' = throw one treat. 'Scatter' = throw 4 or more.
Example: release off a contact with 'Okay' then 'Find' (throw forward); next throw a treat behind the board so you can reload the target plate and the dog can re-load into 2on2off.
tips: Match treat value to how high the distractions are.

skills.name: It's Your Choice (the 'Mugging' game)
skills.purpose: Self-control taught through body language only: the treats are available when the dog stops trying to take them.
how_to: Hold several small treats on an open palm in front of the dog.
If the dog grabs, nuzzles, paws or chews: just close your hand into a fist. Don't pull away. Say NOTHING; no verbal correction.
Open again. When the dog doesn't go for the treats, mark 'Yes' and, with your other hand, take one treat off the palm and feed it.
Repeat, rewarding every right choice.

progressions.text: Move the open hand around: up, down, to the side.
Sit on the floor beside the dog; put 1 treat on the floor by its paws. Cover it with your hand if the dog goes for it; when it stops, pick the treat up and feed with 'Yes'.
Dog in a sit or down. Treat on the floor in front; then on 1 paw, 2 paws, multiple treats. Raise treat value.
How many treats can you put on the paws/floor before 'Yes'? (class challenge)
Use it for stays: dog in sit/down/stand, open hand, step sideways. If they break, close hand and reset; if they hold, return and reward with 'Yes'.
How far can you go: laterally, in front, behind?

tips: Timing matters: open and close your hand at the right moment by reading body language. Dogs have about 1 second to connect a consequence.
Dogs respond to body language first and words second. Less is more: say nothing during this game.
The crate-door game is 'another It's Your Choice game' (Week 3).

skills.name: Leave it
skills.purpose: Don't touch that: food on the floor, a sock, a toy. A safety skill (e.g. broken glass with food on the kitchen floor), and later used in agility when a toy on the ground is the reward.
how_to: Lead your dog to a food container (or a toy) and let them sniff.
Say 'Leave It' to redirect them, then feed a yummy treat from you.
Repeat a few times.
Then play 'This and That': say 'Ready'... 'Get It' and let them have it, so they learn the difference between not allowed and allowed.

progressions.text: Increase temptation: open the food container.

tips: Real-life payoff: food dropped on a broken-glass kitchen floor. 'Leave It' buys time to put the dogs somewhere safe.
In agility, a toy on the ground is often the reward after the dog does something right; 'Leave It' keeps them from self-rewarding.

skills.name: 'Ready' / 'Get It' & 'This and That'
skills.purpose: Permission words. 'Ready' means get ready, look ahead and focus; 'Get It' means go ahead and take it. Builds excitement, self-control, and stops self-rewarding.
how_to: Hold your dog's collar with one hand and a treat about 2 ft from their face in the other.
Say 'Ready'. When they're focused, release with 'Get It'.
'This and That': after a few 'Leave It' reps with a food container, say 'Ready'... 'Get It' and let them have it.
Use the same words for toys.
tips: Use the words consistently. They tell the dog to focus and give permission to go.

skills.name: Crate games ('Your In, Your Out')
skills.purpose: Make the crate a happy, safe place to drive into and wait in. Useful for class, trials, travel, and visiting.
equipment: crate (take the pad out at first so treats are easy to find)
how_to: Throw a couple of treats to the back of the crate.
As soon as they're eaten, release the dog by throwing a treat outside the crate (or reward coming out with a quick tug).

progressions.text: Build speed in and out. Once the dog drives in fast, add the verbal cue.
Make the dog wait a minute inside before releasing.
Close the door for a minute, then open and release. If the dog tries to leave before release, the door closes. No 'No'; it's another It's Your Choice game.
Do it without words, and with gates and doors as well as crates.

troubleshooting: Nervous or crate-shy dog: feed every meal at the back of the crate with the door open and let them choose to go in (F02).
tips: Video: https://youtu.be/FQ7evQmSWYk

skills.name: Sit & position stays
skills.purpose: Respond to the first cue and hold the position until released.
how_to: Ask 'Sit' once at your side; if needed, lure into position with no extra hand signals.
Don't say 'Stay'/'Wait': the position itself means hold it until released.
Reward often while the dog is in position, then slowly build duration.
Add distance using the It's Your Choice open hand (see its progressions).

progressions.text: Puppy: sit, open hand with treats nearest the pup, one small sideways step. Break = close hand and reset; hold = step back, feed, 'Yes, Good Puppy'.
See how far you can go: sideways, in front, behind.

skills.name: Puppy management at home
skills.purpose: Set the puppy up to make good choices outside the crate.
how_to: House leash on whenever the puppy is out, so you can calmly guide/redirect.
Supervise constantly; limit space (e.g. one room with a baby gate).
Manage schedule and behaviours as they come up.
Do many tiny training sessions through the day, e.g. potty breaks with a 'Hurry Up' cue; praise/pet/treat when they go.

skills.name: Play & Settle
skills.purpose: Teach a puppy to switch from excited play to calm, and to play with you appropriately (bite control).
how_to: Play on your knees (taller = safer from face-biting). Gently push the pup away, wiggle fingers, provoke play.
Before the pup gets too wound up: hand in the collar (and hold the leash so they can't grab it), say 'Settle'.
When they relax, release collar pressure, say 'Yes', feed, and keep praising quietly ('Good boy, nice').
Restart play, then settle again before it escalates. Short spurts.

progressions.text: Use it whenever the pup gets over-excited and nips.
Add more distractions; use during Meet & Greet.

tips: No food in your hand while playing; it turns play into wanting the food.
If the pup grabs the leash, take it away and redirect to play with you.

skills.name: Collar grab
skills.purpose: Make being caught rewarding, so the dog doesn't dodge when you reach for it. It's also the start of the drive/focus games.
how_to: Touch/hold the collar, then reward.
Say the dog's name, hold the collar with a bit of pressure, feed, release the collar.

progressions.text: Touch/hold collar > treat.
Name > hold with light pressure > feed > release.
Collar Grab to Hand: hold collar, treat in your other hand ~2 ft from the face. 'Ready'... 'Get It' and release to the hand.
Collar Grab to Target Plate (see Target plate).
Puppy husbandry: collar grab plus handling ears, teeth, feet. If they wiggle, keep holding and say 'Settle'; reward when they relax. Best when pup is a bit tired.
Hold front and back feet, spread toes as if trimming nails; then introduce the clippers (touch, clipping sound).

skills.name: Collar & body hold
skills.purpose: A secure restraint hold for vet exams and handling; also helps with puppy biting.
how_to: One hand runs over the back and under the tummy; the other under the neck and up toward the ear.
Hold the pup securely against your body for just a moment, talking calmly ('Good puppy, well done').
If calm and relaxed: put down, 'Yes', reward. Don't wait for wiggling; if they wiggle, try again and release sooner after they go still.
Optional: a helper rewards while you hold.
Gradually lengthen the hold. Goal: a secure, relaxed 'limp noodle'.

skills.name: Meet & greet a person
skills.purpose: Stay calm when a new person approaches.
how_to: Step 1: Walk the pup toward a seated person who ignores it. At any lunge/jump, collar grab and 'Settle'; when calm, release pressure, 'Good puppy', treat.
Step 2: Pup in sit/stand/down; a person (no dog) walks toward you. If the pup gets excited, hand in collar and 'Settle'; reward calm.
If the pup won't settle: step on the leash and let the pup self-correct, no words; praise and treat the moment they settle.
Visitor takes another step with each success, until they can stand and chat. Later the visitor may offer a treat if the pup stays calm.

skills.name: Name Game (response to name)
skills.purpose: The dog snaps its head to you when it hears its name. This is the first 'recall' a puppy learns.
how_to: Pre-load 5–8 treats in your hand. Sitting/standing doesn't matter; this isn't obedience.
Wait until the dog is NOT looking at you, then say its name once.
The instant the head flicks toward you, feed.
Repeat & treat.

progressions.text: No distractions > gradually add distractions, close and at distance.
Aim for an instant head flick; jackpot (3–4 treats) a great response.
Add motion: say name and back up; let the pup catch up, then feed.

tips: Name = 'head check' (look at me and wait for the next instruction), not 'come here'. In agility the name is a redirect.
Have a throwaway cue too, so the name never gets 'spoiled'.
Great for waiting your turn in class.

skills.name: Informal 'throwaway' cue
skills.purpose: Protect the value of the name and the formal recall by having a casual word for when success isn't likely or you aren't prepared to reward.
how_to: Pick a short fun sound, e.g. high-pitched 'pup pup pup' or a kissing noise.
Use it to engage lightly when the dog may not respond to its name.

skills.name: Formal recall: 'Here' / 'Come'
skills.purpose: Emergency-level cue: come right to me, fast. Possibly lifesaving.
how_to: Use ONLY with great rewards.
With multiple dogs: name first (gets that dog's head check), then 'Here'.
Train it with restrained recalls.

skills.name: Restrained recall
skills.purpose: Build a fast, excited recall to a specific side.
how_to: Helper holds the dog. Step out about 30 ft (food-motivated dogs: show food first).
Without turning your body, look over your right shoulder (show your cheek), say the name, then immediately 'Here'/'Come'.
As you call, drop your right hand by your side and show the toy, so the dog comes to your right side.
On arrival: tug party (or jackpot several treats, excited voice).
Practise both sides.

progressions.text: Puppy version: hold pup, handler runs away. Run > call name > 'Here'/'Come'. Look over your shoulder to the side you want.
Restrained recall into a blind cross (see Blind cross on the flat).

skills.name: Mat work ('Go to bed')
skills.purpose: Going to the mat means lie down and relax until released.
how_to: Lure onto the bed/mat while saying 'Go on your bed'. 'Yes' and treat when on it; 'Good' while they stay.
Release BEFORE the pup leaves: show a treat, throw it 2–3 ft away, say 'OK'.

progressions.text: Lure into a down on the mat (don't cue 'down'); the mat should come to mean 'lie down'. Feed in position, then hold collar, throw a treat, release quickly before they break.
Build time in a down; give a Kong/bone to settle for a few minutes (supervise). Always release from the down with a thrown treat and 'OK'.

tips: Don't cue 'down' on the mat. Lure into the down so the mat itself comes to mean 'lie down and relax'.

skills.name: Loose leash walking
skills.purpose: Walk with a loose 'J' in the leash.
how_to: Start somewhere quiet (a hallway is ideal).
Pup on one side; leash in the opposite hand so it hangs in a 'J' from the collar. Treats in the hand nearest the pup (or a pouch on that hip).
Walk briskly, like you're late.
The moment the pup passes your hip, turn 180°, encouraging with 'pup pup pup'.
When they follow, 'Yes' and treat.
At first you may get only a couple of steps before turning; gradually go further.

progressions.text: Once successful, move to more distracting places (e.g. back yard).

skills.name: Tug & 'Out' (toy exchange)
skills.purpose: Teach the dog to play with you, tug, and let go on cue.
equipment: 2 toys the dog loves (two identical ones if the pup prefers one)
how_to: Play on your knees (discourages face-biting). Wiggle the toy on the ground; push the pup away a little to make it more exciting.
Tug a few times, then stop and present the second toy while saying 'Out'. Hide the first toy behind your back if needed.
Repeat for a minute or two; stop before the pup tires or loses interest.
If teeth hit hand/clothes: hand in collar to stop (a toneless 'Ouch' or a Play & Settle), then restart. Biting ends the game.

progressions.text: Adult dogs: let the dog bring the toy, tug a bit first, then 'Out' and trade for high-value food or another toy.
Control the game: dog/toy on a lead or long line, or train in a hallway. Don't let the dog self-reward by running off with the toy.
Next: 'Put It in My Hand'. The toy is delivered to your hand, not dropped a few feet away.

skills.name: Building toy drive (Week 5 handout)
skills.purpose: Create a dog that loves a special toy, for rewarding at a distance (sends, weaves, gambles).
equipment: throwable toy that doesn't roll much (tug rope, ball in a sock, stuffie)
a special drawer to keep it in
how_to: Keep the toy in a drawer in your main living area. The dog only sees it during this routine (and later at class).
Before meals, act goofy and say silly things on your way to the drawer; slowly open it.
Pause, then whip the toy out like you found $50 and run with it into the next room.
Swing and drag it on the line like a fishing lure, having a great time, but don't let the dog get it at first.
After 1–2 minutes, rush it back to the drawer ('oh no, it's gone') and carry on as normal.
Repeat 2–3 times a day. After day 2, allow a few seconds' grab, playfully steal it back via the line, play alone a bit, put it away.
Gradually lengthen real tug games with you.
tips: From 'How to Create a Motivating Toy' by Susan Garrett, handed out in Foundation Week 5.
Food-mad, toy-indifferent dogs: simmer the toy in liver or chicken broth, but NEVER leave the dog alone with it.
Be sincerely having fun or it won't work. No cues for anything during the routine.
Remove other toys while doing this; leave only chews. Works especially well with puppies.

skills.name: Luring onto objects & new surfaces
skills.purpose: Confidence on different textures and objects; the foundation for perch work and contacts.
equipment: contact board, a piece of cardboard, or an exercise platform
how_to: Lure the dog onto and across the new surface; give lots of cookies even for trying.
Lure onto other objects and slowly increase the time they stay on.
Use 'Good' to say keep going, then 'Yes' and reward when the exercise is over.

progressions.text: Lure onto more objects; longer duration.
Practise positions (sit, down, stand) on the surface, luring if needed and adding the word.

tips: Builds confidence; it's the first step toward perch work and contacts.

skills.name: Perch work & moving off pressure
skills.purpose: Teach the dog it has a back end it can move independently while the front feet stay put, and to move away from handler pressure.
how_to: Start once your dog happily stands on novel objects for a few seconds.
Lure, or shape with the clicker, the two front feet onto the perch.
Step into your dog. The pressure moves their hind end away from you while the front feet stay on.
When the hind end moves, say 'Yes' (or click) and reward.
Start with one step; over time build to a full circle.
Practise both clockwise and anti-clockwise.
tips: Builds rear-end awareness, muscle tone, and balance on both sides.
Teaches the dog that it has a front end and a back end, and to move away from handler pressure.

skills.name: Contact training: 2on2off
skills.purpose: Stop at the bottom of a contact (dogwalk, teeter, A-frame): back feet in the yellow zone, front feet on the ground, until released.
how_to: Sit on the ground in front of (later beside) the plank.
Lure the dog onto the plank with a treat at its nose.
Slowly bring your hand to the ground close to the plank so the front paws step down.
Praise and place a treat between the front paws; keep feeding there, with a new treat ready before the mouth is empty.
While the dog eats, move your hand away from the nose and back.
If the dog leaves, stop talking and lure back into position.
After a few treats, when the dog looks at you, say the release word and drop/throw a treat away from the plank.
tips: Introduce the release word from day one.
Find the distance from the plank where the position is easy to hold.
Hand targeting is the beginning of contact work (F12).

skills.name: What flatwork is & why it matters
skills.purpose: Flatwork is everything between the obstacles: where you set up each approach and do most of your handling.
how_to: Teach handling maneuvers without obstacles first, so your body cues become clear, consistent, coherent and timely.
Foundation flatwork includes restrained recalls, circle work, handling cues with one jump, and target plate work.

skills.name: Circle work (shadow handling)
skills.purpose: Build value for the dog's position at your side (the 'reinforcement zone') at any speed.
equipment: an object to circle: chair, tree, barrel, pylon
spatula with peanut butter etc. for small dogs
how_to: Walk a circle around an object with the dog on the OUTSIDE. Clockwise = dog on your left.
Loose leash in the right hand; treats in the hand nearest the dog (tie the leash around your waist if feeding is awkward).
Feed constantly for correct position. High rate of reinforcement.
After 5–6 treats, break off and play (little tug games are good stress breaks).
Work both directions. No verbal corrections.

progressions.text: Walk, dog on the outside, lots of food.
Add speed on the outside; add straight-line parallel work.
Inside circles at a walk (more pressure; the dog may cut in front or behind). Be patient, break with play, then add speed.
Outside + inside on a loose leash; build speed when ready.

success_criteria: Dog stays at your side, body aligned forward, through acceleration and deceleration.
No forging, lagging, bouncing, pushing your line, or shaping the circle.
No crossing in front (flanking), behind (blind crossing), spinning, or flicking away. Watch especially for swinging wide when you slow down.
tips: Be consistent all day: don't let the dog practise crossing your path or flicking away even when walking to/from the car or kennel (F03).
Small dogs: stay upright; don't bend over to feed.
Video: Shape Up Agility circle work https://youtu.be/6OHVdhE9DqY

skills.name: Target plate: value & sends
skills.purpose: Teach the dog to look and drive ahead, independently of the handler, so you're free to handle.
how_to: Load the plate with food 2–3 ft away.
Collar grab, say 'Ready' (= look ahead).
When the dog flips its head to the plate, release with 'Get It' and race the dog to the plate.
Move the plate further away as drive and speed grow.

progressions.text: Collar grab > Ready > head flips to plate > Get It.

Send with handler motion: lead out ~6 ft, look over your shoulder, dog-side arm back; release ('Get It'/'OK'), swing the arm forward to send. As the dog passes you, move forward with it. Goal: the dog runs PAST you while you're moving.

45° angle: lead out ~10 ft at 45° to the dog and plate. Look over your shoulder, upper body turned, dog-side leg and arm back, shake cookie fingers. Release 'OK', draw the dog around that side, then send to the plate.
Practise straight, 45° and 90° sends.
Review handling to the plate at 45° and 90°.

skills.name: Blind cross on the flat (with restrained recall)
skills.purpose: Handler changes sides in front of the dog; the dog switches sides behind the handler's back.
how_to: A helper holds the dog while you move forward.
Treat or toy in each hand, hands pointing down and slightly out at hip height.
Look to the side you want the dog on ('power of the cheek') and call its name. That arm guides until the dog commits to it.
After commitment, turn your head to the opposite side where you want the dog next.
Reward the dog at the hand that's out.

skills.name: Lap turn (cookie fingers)
skills.purpose: Turn the dog 180° away from you. Dogs naturally turn toward the handler, so this builds body awareness, two-sidedness, lead changes and following handling.
how_to: Treat at the dog's nose height. Back up shaking cookie fingers so the dog follows your hand.
As the dog reaches you, keep drawing it past your hip, then turn it away by rotating your wrist (left hand = clockwise, right hand = counter-clockwise).
Once it commits to the turn, you both move forward, parallel. Feed.
Start slow; add speed once smooth. Practise both sides.

progressions.text: On the flat: back up, turn 180°, move forward and feed.
When turning is easy, throw a ball/toy forward so the dog powers out.
Add speed; throw the toy forward and keep moving parallel; tug at the toy.
Smooth the turn, all 4 feet on the ground; try to beat the dog to the toy.

Around a cone/wing: dog on your left, face the dog, cookie fingers low by the left knee; back toward the cone. Turn the dog away (clockwise) around the cone. Your dog-side (left) leg and arm go BACK while you wait for commitment; feed if the dog struggles to commit. Then move forward parallel and throw the toy (right hand) on the dog's path. Repeat on the right side.

Around an obstacle: start facing each other, guiding arm low, wait for commitment, reward tight turns. Then send from further away. Goal: 2–15 ft without going to the obstacle's plane, while staying connected.

tips: Diagram: Week 13 lap turn steps 1–3 (lap_turn_week13_diagram.gif). Video: Week 13 Lap Turn.

skills.name: Wrap (180° around an obstacle from the front)
skills.purpose: The dog drives forward to an obstacle and wraps tightly back around it.
how_to: Handler and dog face the same direction.
Send forward with your guiding (dog-side) arm and leg, hand kept low.
Wait for the dog to commit ('lock on'/'hook onto' the obstacle) before moving ahead. Be patient.
When smooth, throw a toy ahead so the dog powers out; tug.
Build send distance to 2–15 ft without going to the obstacle's plane.
tips: Video: Week 14 Wrap.

skills.name: Staying connected & rewarding from the non-guiding hand
skills.purpose: Balance handler focus with obstacle commitment so you can stay ahead of your dog.
how_to: Look at the dog's path; your eyes draw theirs forward.
Stay connected ('power of the cheek'). You don't have to physically see the dog.
No sunglasses when working the dog.
From Week 18: stop holding treats in the guiding (dog-side) hand. Reward from the opposite hand, a target plate/food bowl, or a toy.
tips: A purely handler-focused dog must be escorted to every obstacle, which leaves you behind and pushing from the back. Value for going ahead and committing lets you get to the next obstacle first.

skills.name: Clicker challenge: box & two books
skills.purpose: A body-awareness puzzle: clicker train your dog to stand in a box with all 4 feet, or with front feet on 2 separate objects.
how_to: Review a nose touch on an object first.
Put down a shallow box (or two small books). No words, no luring.
Click & feed for looking at it, stepping toward it, any foot in or on it.
Raise criteria a little at a time: one foot, two feet, then all four (or both front feet on the two books).
Change the challenge each session, and bring your items to class to show what you've been working on.
tips: Builds a thinking dog that offers behaviours, works through a hard task, and gains mental stamina.

cues.meaning: Head check: look at me and wait for the next instruction. Not 'come'.
Informal throwaway attention sound; protects the name.
Correct; exercise over; reward right now.
Keep going, you're doing it right.
Permission to go do it (food, toy, plate).
Deliver the toy to my hand.
Sit and hold it until released (no 'stay' needed).
Go to the mat and lie down.

glossary.definition: The spot at the handler's side where the dog gets rewarded.
Dog crosses in front of the handler, or swings wide and turns to face them when the handler slows.
Dog crosses behind the handler. Unwanted in circle work.
Dog turns/spins away from the handler.
Handler changes sides in front of the dog while the dog switches behind them.
Turning your head/shoulder so the dog sees your cheek, which signals the side you want them on.
Your dog-side hand/arm/leg, used to send and turn.
The dog has locked on to going around/over an obstacle, so the handler can move on.
Several treats at once for an exceptional response.
Rewarding a behaviour the dog does on its own.
Rewarding small successive steps toward a final behaviour.
Rewarding unpredictably once a criterion is learned, to keep the dog trying.
Yellow ends of the dogwalk, teeter and A-frame; at least one paw must touch them.
Hind feet on the contact, front feet on the ground, held until release.
Food, toy and prey motivation. Aim for a balance.
